title: In the Absence of Feedback, the Most Experienced People Presume the Negative
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post argues that silence from a leader is read as criticism, and that this is especially true of tenured, highly skilled team members. Citing coach Pat Summitt, it holds that people fill in the blanks with a negative when feedback is missing. The author targets the common belief that leaving experienced people alone is a reward and that they will ask if they want input. That belief is called faulty, because no one outgrows the need for encouragement, praise and advice from the leader. The closing move is practical: audit how often you tell your most experienced people they are doing exceptional work or offer ideas for growth.
points: Without feedback, team members tend to assume their work is not valued and their performance is merely adequate.
Long-serving leaders and tenured teams are most prone to assuming that people already know where they stand.
Treating non-interference as a reward is a mistake, since experienced people still want the leader's view of their performance.
No one outgrows the need for praise, validation or advice, and only the leader can supply certain kinds of encouragement.
Everyone wants to hear great work when they deliver and here's an idea to try when they do not.
quotes: In the absence of feedback, people often presume they are doing poorly. In the words of legendary coach Pat Summit, they prefer to “fill in the blanks with a negative.

People have a genuine need to know where they stand in the eyes of the leader. Leaders who are reluctant to praise, criticize, or comment on how people are doing sow the seeds of doubt more than they know.

Leaders who have been in the role for a long time and who work with highly tenured team members are especially susceptible to this problem. They, too, often presume people know how they are doing, receive plenty of external feedback, and no longer need the ongoing assessment of the leader to know how well or poorly they are doing.

Even when things are going swimmingly, team members want to hear from the leader about how they see their performance. In the absence of feedback, team members often presume their work is not being valued, their ideas are not of interest, and their performance is only adequate. Imaginations run wild when information about performance is not forthcoming.
Too many leaders believe leaving experienced people alone to do their work is a reward. When people need them or want some feedback, they should be comfortable enough to ask.
Everyone, no matter how skilled and expert, wants to hear “great work” when they deliver and “here’s an idea to try” when they don’t.
Feedback, not the absence of it, is the reward the most experienced team members most desire. No one learns without it.
